claim: The bacterial flagellum consists of three major domains: an ion-driven motor, a hook-basal body, and a hollow filament tube.
source: The highly complex bacterial flagellum consists of three major domains: an ion-driven motor, which can provide torque in either direction; a universal joint called the hook-basal body, which transmits motor torque; and a 20-nm-thick hollow filament tube composed of the flagellin subunit, which acts as a propeller (reviewed in Altegoer and Bange, 2015; Nakamura and Minamino, 2019).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge, supported by citations to review articles.

evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge, supported by citations to review articles.

source: Flagella are costly for the cell to synthesize, requiring up to ~2% of the cell's biosynthetic energy expenditure and extensive use of ribosomes (reviewed in Soutourina and Bertin, 2003; Guttenplan and Kearns, 2013).

claim: Flagella synthesis requires extensive use of ribosomes.
source: Flagella are costly for the cell to synthesize, requiring up to ~2% of the cell's biosynthetic energy expenditure and extensive use of ribosomes (reviewed in Soutourina and Bertin, 2003; Guttenplan and Kearns, 2013).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge, supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Transcription of the genes in the flagellar regulon is activated in a sequential manner in Escherichia coli.
source: To ensure that flagellar components are made in the order in which they are needed, transcription of the genes in the regulon is activated in a sequential manner in Escherichia coli (Kalir et al., 2001) and Salmonella enterica (reviewed in Chevance and Hughes, 2008).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Transcription of the genes in the flagellar regulon is activated in a sequential manner in Salmonella enterica.
source: To ensure that flagellar components are made in the order in which they are needed, transcription of the genes in the regulon is activated in a sequential manner in Escherichia coli (Kalir et al., 2001) and Salmonella enterica (reviewed in Chevance and Hughes, 2008).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge, supported by citations to a review article.

claim: The genes in the flagellar regulon can be divided into three groups based on their time of activation: early genes, middle genes, and late genes.
source: The genes can be divided into three groups based on their time of activation: early genes, middle genes, and late genes (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The FlhDC transcription regulators, encoded by the two early genes, activate the transcription of the middle genes.
source: The FlhDC transcription regulators, encoded by the two early genes, activate the transcription of the middle genes (Class 2), which are required for the hook-basal body.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claim: The middle genes (Class 2) are required for the hook-basal body.
source: The FlhDC transcription regulators, encoded by the two early genes, activate the transcription of the middle genes (Class 2), which are required for the hook-basal body.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claim: FlhDC activates transcription of fliA, encoding sigma factor σ28.
source: FlhDC also activates transcription of fliA, encoding sigma factor σ28 (Fitzgerald et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: σ28 activates transcription of the late genes responsible for completing the flagellum and the chemotaxis system.
source: σ28 in turn activates transcription of the late genes responsible for completing the flagellum and the chemotaxis system (Class 3).

claim: σ28 increases expression of several of the middle genes (Class 2/3).
source: σ28 additionally increases expression of several of the middle genes (Class 2/3) (Fitzgerald et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: σ28 activity is negatively regulated by the anti-sigma factor, FlgM.
source: σ28 activity itself is negatively regulated by the anti-sigma factor, FlgM, which is transported out of the cell, freeing σ28, when the hook-basal body complex is complete (reviewed in Smith and Hoover, 2009; Osterman et al., 2015).

claim: FlgM is transported out of the cell when the hook-basal body complex is complete.
source: σ28 activity itself is negatively regulated by the anti-sigma factor, FlgM, which is transported out of the cell, freeing σ28, when the hook-basal body complex is complete (reviewed in Smith and Hoover, 2009; Osterman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge, supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Various factors can be rate limiting under specific conditions during flagellum assembly.
source: Given the numerous components required at different times and in different stoichiometries during flagellum assembly, various factors can be rate limiting under specific conditions (reviewed in Chevance and Hughes, 2008).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge, supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: The dependence of flagella synthesis on FlhDC and σ28 generates a coherent feed-forward loop.
source: The dependence of flagella synthesis on FlhDC and σ28 generates a coherent feed-forward loop.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claim: In the coherent feed-forward loop, the first regulator (FlhDC) activates the second regulator (σ28), and they both additively activate their target genes.
source: In this loop, the first regulator (FlhDC) activates the second regulator (σ28), and they both additively activate their target genes.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claim: The coherent feed-forward loop results in prolonged flagellar expression, protecting the flagella synthesis from a transient loss of input signal.
source: This results in prolonged flagellar expression, protecting the flagella synthesis from a transient loss of input signal (Kalir et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: The predicted structures for the four σ28-dependent sRNAs are consistent with the structures of known Hfq-binding sRNAs.

claim: UhpU overexpression causes a slight increase in flagella number.
source: UhpU overexpression caused a slight increase in flagella number (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by EM analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: UhpU overexpression causes a marked increase in motility.

claim: MotR overexpression leads to a dramatic increase in the flagella number.

claim: MotR* overexpression does not have a significant effect on motility.

claim: FliX-S overexpression reduces bacterial motility.

claim: FliX overexpression does not reduce bacterial motility.

claim: FlgO overexpression does not result in detectable changes in flagella number or motility.

claim: MotR and FliX overexpression have only slight effects on growth.

claim: LrhA represses flhDC transcription.

claim: ArcZ and RprA increase rpoS expression.
source: Intriguingly, ArcZ, RprA, and LrhA form a complex regulatory network with the general stress response sigma factor σS encoded by rpoS, as previous studies showed that LrhA represses the expression of rprA and rpoS (Peterson et al., 2006), while ArcZ and RprA increase rpoS expression (reviewed in Mika and Hengge, 2014).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge, supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: The high numbers of chimeras between UhpU, MotR or FliX with the fliC mRNA encoding flagellin were striking.
source: The high numbers of chimeras between UhpU, MotR or FliX with the fliC mRNA encoding flagellin were striking, particularly between the 3´ end of fliC corresponding to FliX (blue) and the 5´ end of fliC (red) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by RIL-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Most of the chimeras between UhpU, MotR or FliX and fliC were internal to the fliC CDS.
source: As mentioned above, it was also noteworthy that most of the chimeras were internal to the fliC CDS.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by RIL-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: UhpU overexpression leads to somewhat increased levels of flagellin, both as cytosolic monomers and de-polymerized flagella.
source: When we examined the consequences of overexpressing UhpU, MotR, MotR*, FliX or FliX-S on the levels of the flagellin protein, we observed somewhat increased levels of flagellin, both as cytosolic monomers (Figure 4B) and de-polymerized flagella (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) with UhpU and MotR* overexpression
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MotR* overexpression leads to somewhat increased levels of flagellin, both as cytosolic monomers and de-polymerized flagella.
source: When we examined the consequences of overexpressing UhpU, MotR, MotR*, FliX or FliX-S on the levels of the flagellin protein, we observed somewhat increased levels of flagellin, both as cytosolic monomers (Figure 4B) and de-polymerized flagella (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) with UhpU and MotR* overexpression
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: FliX overexpression leads to reduced levels of flagellin.
source: and reduced levels with FliX or FliX-S overexpression.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: FliX-S overexpression leads to reduced levels of flagellin.
source: and reduced levels with FliX or FliX-S overexpression.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: UhpU overexpression leads to increased levels of the fliC mRNA.
source: These differences are reflected in increased levels of the fliC mRNA with overexpression of UhpU, particularly in a crl+ background, or MotR or MotR*, particularly at OD600~0.2 (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: MotR overexpression leads to increased levels of the fliC mRNA.
source: These differences are reflected in increased levels of the fliC mRNA with overexpression of UhpU, particularly in a crl+ background, or MotR or MotR*, particularly at OD600~0.2 (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: MotR* overexpression leads to increased levels of the fliC mRNA.
source: These differences are reflected in increased levels of the fliC mRNA with overexpression of UhpU, particularly in a crl+ background, or MotR or MotR*, particularly at OD600~0.2 (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: fliC mRNA levels decreased with FliX overexpression.
source: In contrast, fliC mRNA levels decreased with FliX and FliX-S overexpression (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: fliC mRNA levels decreased with FliX-S overexpression.
source: In contrast, fliC mRNA levels decreased with FliX and FliX-S overexpression (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The impacts of the sRNAs on flagellin protein and fliC mRNA levels are consistent with the increased flagella number and/or motility upon UhpU or MotR overexpression and decreased flagella number upon FliX overexpression.
source: In general, the impacts of the sRNAs on flagellin protein and fliC mRNA levels are consistent with the increased flagella number and/or motility upon UhpU or MotR overexpression and decreased flagella number upon FliX overexpression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective findings of the study.

claim: Changes in cleavage patterns due to the presence of UhpU, which overlap regions of predicted base pairing, were observed in in vitro footprinting experiments.
source: Changes in cleavage patterns due to the presence of an sRNA, which overlap regions of predicted base pairing, are indicated by the thick red brackets.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by in vitro footprinting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Changes in cleavage patterns due to the presence of MotR, which overlap regions of predicted base pairing, were observed in in vitro footprinting experiments.
source: Changes in cleavage patterns due to the presence of an sRNA, which overlap regions of predicted base pairing, are indicated by the thick red brackets.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by in vitro footprinting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Changes in cleavage patterns due to the presence of FliX-S, which overlap regions of predicted base pairing, were observed in in vitro footprinting experiments.
source: Changes in cleavage patterns due to the presence of an sRNA, which overlap regions of predicted base pairing, are indicated by the thick red brackets.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by in vitro footprinting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Hfq-dependent changes were observed in the region from ~+40 to+66 from the fliC AUG.
source: We also observed Hfq dependent changes (black bracket) in the region from ~+40 to+66 from the fliC AUG, which is enriched for ARN motif sequences (AAA, AAT, AAC, AAG, AAC), known to be important for mRNA binding to the distal face of Hfq binding (reviewed in Updegrove et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by in vitro footprinting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The region from ~+40 to+66 from the fliC AUG is enriched for ARN motif sequences.
source: We also observed Hfq dependent changes (black bracket) in the region from ~+40 to+66 from the fliC AUG, which is enriched for ARN motif sequences (AAA, AAT, AAC, AAG, AAC), known to be important for mRNA binding to the distal face of Hfq binding (reviewed in Updegrove et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by sequence analysis.

claim: ARN motif sequences are known to be important for mRNA binding to the distal face of Hfq binding.
source: We also observed Hfq dependent changes (black bracket) in the region from ~+40 to+66 from the fliC AUG, which is enriched for ARN motif sequences (AAA, AAT, AAC, AAG, AAC), known to be important for mRNA binding to the distal face of Hfq binding (reviewed in Updegrove et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge, supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Both MotR and the MotR-M1 mutant RNAs led to additional protection at another region and increased cleavage at other positions.
source: Additionally, we noted that both MotR and the MotR-M1 mutant RNAs led to additional protection at another region (thin red bracket) and increased cleavage (red asterisks) at other positions and suggesting a second region of MotR base pairing with fliC as well as MotR-induced structure changes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by in vitro footprinting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The fliC sequence from ~+40 to~+170 is more structured than the surrounding regions.
source: In general, the differences in cleavage by RNase III (preference for double-stranded RNA) and lead (preference for single-stranded RNA), indicate the fliC sequence from ~+40 to~+170 is more structured than the surrounding regions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro footprinting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Genes encoding ribosomal proteins were among the top MotR and FliX targets in the RIL-seq data sets.
source: Given that genes encoding ribosomal proteins were among the top MotR and FliX targets in the RIL-seq data sets and were not detected for many other sRNAs (Supplementary file 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), we investigated MotR and FliX regulation of these genes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by RIL-seq data shown in Supplementary file 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Genes encoding ribosomal proteins were not detected as targets for many other sRNAs.
source: Given that genes encoding ribosomal proteins were among the top MotR and FliX targets in the RIL-seq data sets and were not detected for many other sRNAs (Supplementary file 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), we investigated MotR and FliX regulation of these genes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by RIL-seq data shown in Supplementary file 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Several of the top interactions for MotR and FliX in the RIL-seq data mapped to the essential S10 operon, within the CDSs.
source: Several of the top interactions for MotR and FliX in the RIL-seq data mapped to the essential S10 operon, again within the CDSs (Figure 5 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by RIL-seq data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The co-transcriptional regulation of the S10 operon has been studied extensively.
source: The co-transcriptional regulation of the S10 operon has been studied extensively (Zengel and Lindahl, 1996; Zengel et al., 2002; Zengel and Lindahl, 1992).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: The leader sequence upstream of the first gene rpsJ encoding S10 is bound by the ribosomal protein L4, encoded by the third gene in the operon (rplD), causing transcription termination.
source: The leader sequence upstream of the first gene rpsJ encoding S10 is bound by the ribosomal protein L4, encoded by the third gene in the operon (rplD), causing transcription termination, thus modulating the levels of all the ribosomal proteins in the operon in response to the levels of unincorporated L4.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claim: L4 binding modulates the levels of all the ribosomal proteins in the S10 operon in response to the levels of unincorporated L4.
source: The leader sequence upstream of the first gene rpsJ encoding S10 is bound by the ribosomal protein L4, encoded by the third gene in the operon (rplD), causing transcription termination, thus modulating the levels of all the ribosomal proteins in the operon in response to the levels of unincorporated L4.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claim: L4 binding specifically inhibits translation of rpsJ.
source: L4 binding also has been shown to specifically inhibit translation of rpsJ, an effect that can be genetically distinguished from the L4 effect on transcription termination (Freedman et al., 1987).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: MotR overexpression elevated the expression of the rpsJ-gfp fusion.
source: MotR overexpression elevated the expression of the rpsJ-gfp fusion, and MotR* enhanced this effect (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by GFP reporter assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: MotR* enhanced the effect of MotR on the expression of the rpsJ-gfp fusion.
source: MotR overexpression elevated the expression of the rpsJ-gfp fusion, and MotR* enhanced this effect (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by GFP reporter assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Positive regulation of S10 expression by MotR and MotR* was observed by immunoblot analysis of an N-terminal FLAG-tagged S10 protein.
source: Positive regulation of S10 expression by MotR and MotR* was similarly observed by immunoblot analysis of an N-terminal FLAG-tagged S10 protein encoded along with the S10 leader behind the heterologous promoter on a pBAD plasmid (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: A mutation in the MotR seed sequence (MotR-M1 and MotR*-M1) eliminated the up-regulation of the FLAG-tagged S10.
source: A mutation in the MotR seed sequence (MotR-M1 and MotR*-M1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) eliminated the up-regulation of the FLAG-tagged S10 (Figure 5D)
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: A mutation in the MotR seed sequence eliminated the MotR effect on flagella number.
source: A mutation in the MotR seed sequence (MotR-M1 and MotR*-M1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) eliminated the up-regulation of the FLAG-tagged S10 (Figure 5D) and the MotR effect on flagella number (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by EM data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The RNase T1, RNase III and lead cleavage assays supported the position of the predicted base-pairing between MotR and rpsJ mRNA.
source: The RNase T1, RNase III and lead cleavage assays supported the position of the predicted base-pairing between MotR and rpsJ mRNA (red and blue brackets), indicating MotR binds to rpsJ at ~+150 nt in its CDS.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by in vitro footprinting data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: MotR binds to rpsJ at ~+150 nt in its CDS.
source: The RNase T1, RNase III and lead cleavage assays supported the position of the predicted base-pairing between MotR and rpsJ mRNA (red and blue brackets), indicating MotR binds to rpsJ at ~+150 nt in its CDS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vitro footprinting data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Hfq binds to the attenuator hairpin in the S10 leader sequence.
source: Again, we detected Hfq binding (black bracket), here to the attenuator hairpin in the S10 leader sequence (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), which has three ARN sequences (AGG, AGU and AAC).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by in vitro footprinting data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The attenuator hairpin in the S10 leader sequence has three ARN sequences (AGG, AGU and AAC).
source: Again, we detected Hfq binding (black bracket), here to the attenuator hairpin in the S10 leader sequence (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), which has three ARN sequences (AGG, AGU and AAC).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by sequence analysis.

claim: The M1 mutation eliminated binding in the predicted region of pairing between MotR and rpsJ.
source: The M1 mutation eliminated binding in the predicted region of pairing but a complementary mutation in the corresponding region of rpsJ mRNA did not restore MotR binding (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by in vitro footprinting data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A complementary mutation in the corresponding region of rpsJ mRNA did not restore MotR binding.
source: The M1 mutation eliminated binding in the predicted region of pairing but a complementary mutation in the corresponding region of rpsJ mRNA did not restore MotR binding (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by in vitro footprinting data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: MotR-dependent regulation was eliminated for rpsJ-gfp fusions that removed the S10 leader sequence, stem D, or the attenuator hairpin stem E.
source: MotR-dependent regulation was eliminated for each of these constructs suggesting that S10 leader sequence is needed along with the MotR binding site internal to the rpsJ CDS for MotR-dependent regulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by GFP reporter assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: S10 leader sequence is needed along with the MotR binding site internal to the rpsJ CDS for MotR-dependent regulation.
source: MotR-dependent regulation was eliminated for each of these constructs suggesting that S10 leader sequence is needed along with the MotR binding site internal to the rpsJ CDS for MotR-dependent regulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GFP reporter assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MotR no longer upregulates rpsJ-gfp in the HfqY25D mutant background.
source: Supporting a role for Hfq, MotR, which is present at the same levels in the Hfq WT and HfqY25D mutant strains, no longer upregulates rpsJ-gfp in the distal face mutant background (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by GFP reporter assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: MotR is present at the same levels in the Hfq WT and HfqY25D mutant strains.
source: Supporting a role for Hfq, MotR, which is present at the same levels in the Hfq WT and HfqY25D mutant strains, no longer upregulates rpsJ-gfp in the distal face mutant background (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: FliX interacts with multiple regions in the S10 operon mRNA, all internal to CDSs.
source: Based on the RIL-seq data, FliX interacts with multiple regions in the S10 operon mRNA, all internal to CDSs (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by RIL-seq data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The predicted base-pairing regions between FliX and the S10 operon align with the highest peaks of chimeras in the RIL-seq data.
source: The predicted base-pairing regions (Figure 5G) align with the highest peaks of chimeras in the RIL-seq data and overlap with the seed sequence suggested for FliX (Melamed et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by RIL-seq data and base pairing predictions shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The predicted base-pairing regions between FliX and the S10 operon overlap with the seed sequence suggested for FliX.
source: The predicted base-pairing regions (Figure 5G) align with the highest peaks of chimeras in the RIL-seq data and overlap with the seed sequence suggested for FliX (Melamed et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by RIL-seq data, base pairing predictions shown in Figure 5G, and a citation.

claim: Overproduction of FliX or FliX-S led to a reduction in the expression of rplC-gfp, rpsQ-gfp, and rpsS-rplV-gfp fusions.
source: We tested the effects of FliX on expression from this operon by constructing gfp fusions to regions of rplC, rpsQ, and rpsS-rplV. In all cases, overproduction of FliX or FliX-S led to a reduction in the expression of these fusions (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by GFP reporter assay data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The regions that were changed in rpsS and FliX-S in the in vitro footprinting aligned with the predicted binding region between the two RNAs.
source: To test for a direct interaction between FliX-S and the rpsS mRNA, we again carried out structure probing (Figure 5I and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D). The regions that were changed in rpsS and FliX-S in the in vitro footprinting aligned with the predicted binding region between the two RNAs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by in vitro footprinting data shown in Figure 5I and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: Introduction of the M1 mutation eliminated FliX-S binding to the rpsS mRNA.
source: Introduction of the M1 mutation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) eliminated FliX-S binding to the rpsS mRNA while introduction of a complementary mutation in the rpsS mRNA restored FliX-S-M1 binding (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by in vitro footprinting data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Introduction of a complementary mutation in the rpsS mRNA restored FliX-S-M1 binding.
source: Introduction of the M1 mutation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) eliminated FliX-S binding to the rpsS mRNA while introduction of a complementary mutation in the rpsS mRNA restored FliX-S-M1 binding (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by in vitro footprinting data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: In vivo primer extension assays showed an increase in 5´ ends in proximity to the binding site on the rpsS mRNA in FliX or FliX-S overexpressing strains.
source: Further experiments are needed to test this model, but in vivo primer extension assays carried out for RNA isolated from in mid-log phase cells (OD600 ~0.6) showed an increase in 5´ ends in proximity to the binding site on the rpsS mRNA in FliX or FliX-S overexpressing strains (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by primer extension data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The S10 protein encoded by rpsJ has two roles in the cell: it is incorporated into the 30S ribosome subunit and it forms a transcription anti-termination complex with NusB.
source: The S10 protein encoded by rpsJ has two roles in the cell. It is incorporated into the 30S ribosome subunit but also forms a transcription anti-termination complex with NusB (Lüttgen et al., 2002; Luo et al., 2008; Baniulyte et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Cells carrying the S10Δloop plasmid had higher number of flagella like cells overexpressing MotR*.
source: First, we overexpressed a S10 mutant (S10Δloop) that is missing the ribosome binding loop but is still active in anti-termination (Luo et al., 2008) from an inducible plasmid and analyzed the number of flagella per cell. Cells carrying the S10Δloop plasmid had higher number of flagella like cells overexpressing MotR* (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by EM data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Overexpression of wild type S10 from the plasmid used for overexpression of S10∆loop did not lead to an increase in flagella number.
source: We noted that overexpression of wild type S10 from the plasmid used for overexpression of S10∆loop did not lead to an increase in flagella number (Figure 6A)
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by EM data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The stimulatory effect of MotR* on flagella number was eliminated in a ∆nusB strain.
source: Since rpsJ is essential and cannot be deleted, we also examined the effect of MotR* overexpression in a ∆nusB strain that cannot form the S10-NusB anti-termination complex. In this background, the stimulatory effect of MotR* on flagella number was eliminated (Figure 6B)
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by EM data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: S10Δloop overexpression does not increase flagella number in the ∆nusB background.
source: as is also observed for S10Δloop overexpression in the ∆nusB background (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by EM data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MotR and MotR* overexpression increased the mRNA levels of genes in the motAB-cheAW and tar-tap-cheRBYZ operons in WT background.
source: To directly test this anti-termination hypothesis, we carried out RT-qPCR analysis in WT and ∆nusB backgrounds to examine the effects of MotR and MotR* overexpression on genes in the motAB-cheAW and tar-tap-cheRBYZ operons. For both operons, the mRNA levels of the tested genes were increased in WT upon MotR and MotR* overexpression (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MotR and MotR* overexpression did not increase the mRNA levels of the non-flagellar control gene cadB.
source: This increase was not observed for the non-flagellar control gene cadB.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The levels of the flagellar mRNAs in ∆nusB background were lower than in the WT.
source: While the levels of the flagellar mRNAs in ∆nusB background were lower than in the WT, MotR and MotR* no longer induced these genes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MotR and MotR* no longer induced flagellar genes in ∆nusB background.
source: While the levels of the flagellar mRNAs in ∆nusB background were lower than in the WT, MotR and MotR* no longer induced these genes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The transcripts whose levels increased most with MotR* overexpression corresponded predominantly to late genes and, to a lesser extent, middle genes, of the flagellar regulon.
source: The transcripts whose levels increased most with MotR* overexpression compared to the vector control (Figure 7A) corresponded predominantly to late genes and, to a lesser extent, middle genes, of the flagellar regulon.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Of the 332 genes whose expression increased significantly (FDR = 0.05) by MotR* overexpression, 40 are reduced significantly (FDR = 0.05) in a strain lacking σ28 (ΔfliA).
source: Of the 332 genes whose expression increased significantly (FDR = 0.05) by MotR* overexpression, 40 are reduced significantly (FDR = 0.05) in a strain lacking σ28 (ΔfliA) (Fitzgerald et al., 2014; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by RNA-seq data shown in Supplementary file 2 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The sequence motif found for the promoters of the transcription units for which expression increased the most upon MotR* overproduction is nearly identical to a σ28 recognition motif.
source: Additionally, the sequence motif found for the promoters of the transcription units for which expression increased the most (FDR = 0.05 and ≥2 fold) upon MotR* overproduction (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) is nearly identical to a σ28 recognition motif (Fitzgerald et al., 2014; Shi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and citations.

claim: Transcripts for flagellar genes were reduced by FliX overexpression.
source: In contrast, transcripts for flagellar genes were reduced by FliX overexpression (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7B and Supplementary file 2.

claim: 28 of 149 genes for which the expression is reduced significantly (FDR = 0.05) by FliX overexpression are middle or late genes of the flagellar regulon.
source: Specifically, 28 of 149 genes for which the expression is reduced significantly (FDR = 0.05) are middle or late genes of the flagellar regulon (Fitzgerald et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by RNA-seq data shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: MotR and MotR* overexpression increased the activity of the flgB and fliL promoters.
source: The effects of MotR, MotR*, FliX, and FliX-S on flagella gene expression were further examined by monitoring fluorescence from gfp fused to the promoters of flgB, a representative Class 2 promoter, and fliL, a representative Class 2/3 promoter (Zaslaver et al., 2006). MotR and MotR* overexpression increased the activity of the two promoters
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by GFP reporter assay data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: FliX and FliX-S overexpression led to a reduction of the activity of the flgB and fliL promoters.
source: while FliX and FliX-S overexpression led to a reduction of their activity (Figure 7C and D, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by GFP reporter assay data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The levels of C-terminally SPA-tagged FlgJ increased across growth upon MotR* overexpression, particularly early in growth.
source: The levels of C-terminally SPA-tagged FlgJ, also encoded by a Class 2 gene, similarly increased across growth upon MotR* overexpression, particularly early in growth
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The levels of C-terminally SPA-tagged FlgJ decreased upon FliX-S overexpression.
source: and decreased upon FliX-S overexpression (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2D.

claim: MotR-M1 levels were comparable to WT MotR levels.
source: MotR-M1 levels were comparable to WT MotR levels (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The prominent ~200 nt FliX band was reduced for FliX-M1.
source: The prominent ~200 nt FliX band was reduced for FliX-M1, while other FliX processing products were affected less (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by Northern blot data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The motR-M1 chromosomal mutation was associated with a moderate reduction in flagella number at two time points (OD600 ~0.6 and 2.0).
source: The motR-M1 chromosomal mutation was associated with a moderate reduction in flagella number at two time points (OD600 ~0.6 and 2.0) (Figure 8A)
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by EM data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Slightly higher numbers of flagella were observed for the fliX-M1 strain at the later time point (OD600 ~2.0).
source: while slightly higher numbers of flagella were observed for the fliX-M1 strain at the later time point (OD600 ~2.0) (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by EM data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Reduced motility of the motR-M1 strain compared to WT was observed in motility assays.
source: In motility assays carried out as in Figure 2, we found reduced motility of the motR-M1 strain compared to WT but no change was observed for the fliX-M1 strain (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.
